period_summary: Citations are most concentrated in the 2nd through 4th centuries CE, peaking with the Alexandrian and Antiochene schools. This distribution reflects the passage's intense Christological utility in the Logos theology debates and anti-Jewish polemic of that era.

citations.cited_text: For a child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and the government shall be upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the Age to Come, Prince of Peace.
citations.text_form_note: Justin's rendering aligns closely with the LXX title sequence (Θαυμαστός, Σύμβουλος, Θεὸς ἰσχυρός, ἐξουσιαστής, Ἄρχων εἰρήνης), including the LXX's distinctive rendering 'Mighty God' absent in MT's differently structured compound name. The slight paraphrastic quality lowers certainty from HIGH to medium-high.
citations.theological_use: Justin deploys this passage in his proof-from-prophecy argument against Trypho to demonstrate that the divine titles applied to the Messiah in Isaiah anticipate the Incarnation, specifically arguing that 'Mighty God' and 'Father of the Age to Come' can only refer to Christ.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's citation attests an early 2nd-century LXX-type text in circulation in Rome/Syria, substantially conforming to the later Göttingen LXX tradition for Isaiah.

citations.cited_text: His name is called the Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Powerful, Prince of Peace, Father of the World to Come.
citations.text_form_note: Irenaeus includes 'Angel of Great Counsel' (Μεγάλης Βουλῆς Ἄγγελος), a reading found in the LXX tradition (attested in key LXX manuscripts and the Göttingen apparatus) but not in the MT; yet his title order and 'Father of the World to Come' shows partial divergence from the standard LXX, possibly reflecting an Old Latin intermediary or an eclectic Greek text available in Gaul.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses the concatenated divine titles to argue for the unity of Christ's divine and human natures against Gnostic bifurcations, insisting that all these names refer to a single incarnate person, not multiple aeons.
citations.transmission_implication: The inclusion of 'Angel of Great Counsel' suggests Irenaeus used a Greek LXX text or its Old Latin translation that preserved this expanded title, attesting a non-MT expansion already embedded in the LXX Vorlage available in the western church by c. 180 CE.

citations.work: Commentary on Isaiah; also Contra Celsum
citations.chapter_section: Comm. Isa. frag.; Contra Celsum I.56
citations.cited_text: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and his government is upon his shoulder; and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Powerful, Prince of Peace, Father of the Coming Age.
citations.text_form_note: Origen's citation preserves the LXX's 'Angel of Great Counsel' (Μεγάλης Βουλῆς Ἄγγελος) as its first title, precisely the reading found in the main LXX tradition (Codex Vaticanus lineage) and discussed in the Göttingen apparatus, which is entirely absent from the MT; his six-part title sequence is substantially that of the standard LXX.
citations.theological_use: Origen uses this text in Contra Celsum to rebut pagan critiques by arguing that the prophetic precision of Isaiah's divine titles constitutes evidence of divine foreknowledge, and in his homilies to elaborate a Logos-Christology in which 'Angel of Great Counsel' points to the pre-incarnate Son as mediator of the divine will.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's Hexaplaric work on Isaiah means his citation reflects careful comparison with the Hebrew; his retention of 'Angel of Great Counsel' despite its absence from the Hebrew confirms he recognized the LXX expansion but considered it authoritative for the church's text.

citations.cited_text: A child has been born for us, a son given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder; and his name has been called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Powerful, Ruler of Peace, Father of the Age to Come.
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius largely follows the LXX title sequence and wording, though his omission of 'Angel of Great Counsel' (present in Origen and Irenaeus) may reflect his use of Origen's Hexapla and conscious alignment with a hexaplaric recension that had partially corrected toward the Hebrew, or a manuscript variant within the LXX tradition itself.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius cites this passage as one of the central proof-texts in his apologetic demonstration that Hebrew prophecy anticipated Christ, using the royal and divine titles as a structural argument for the divine Logos becoming incarnate.
citations.transmission_implication: Eusebius's variant title list, compared with Origen, suggests that even within the Caesarean school there was not a single fixed LXX text of Isaiah 9:6 in the early 4th century, pointing to live textual pluralism in the LXX manuscript tradition.

citations.cited_text: To us a child is born, and to us a son is given, and the government is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Angel of Great Counsel.
citations.text_form_note: Athanasius cites only the first title 'Angel of Great Counsel,' which is the distinctive LXX reading absent from MT; this selective citation is typical of patristic homiletical focus but is clearly drawn from the LXX textual stream, aligning with the Alexandrian LXX tradition of Isaiah.
citations.theological_use: Athanasius deploys 'Angel of Great Counsel' to argue that the pre-incarnate Son served as divine messenger of the Father's redemptive plan (βουλή), and that the Incarnation fulfills this angelic-mediatorial role, countering Arian attempts to reduce the Son to creaturely status.
citations.transmission_implication: The isolated citation of 'Angel of Great Counsel' by Athanasius confirms this LXX-specific title was a live and familiar reading in 4th-century Alexandria, independently supporting its authenticity within the Egyptian LXX manuscript tradition.

citations.cited_text: Parvulus natus est nobis, filius datus est nobis, et factus est principatus super humerum eius, et vocabitur nomen eius Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis, Pater futuri saeculi, Princeps pacis.
citations.text_form_note: Jerome's Vulgate rendering follows the Hebrew MT tradition in presenting the names as a single compound name for the child-king, without the LXX's 'Angel of Great Counsel'; his five-title sequence (Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis, Pater futuri saeculi, Princeps pacis) corresponds closely to the MT's structure and his iuxta Hebraeos translation principles, consciously departing from the LXX expansion.
citations.theological_use: Jerome uses this passage to argue against what he regards as LXX translational liberties, insisting that the Hebrew original yields a cleaner Christological prophecy; he applies the titles Christologically while critiquing Origen's over-reliance on the LXX's 'Angel' title.
citations.transmission_implication: Jerome's MT-aligned citation represents a deliberate 4th–5th century move toward Hebraica veritas that would permanently divide the western (Vulgate, MT-proximate) and eastern (LXX-based) textual streams for this verse.

citations.cited_text: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given, whose sovereignty rests upon his shoulder; and he shall be called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counsellor, God Mighty, Powerful, Prince of Peace, Father of the World to Come.
citations.text_form_note: Cyril preserves the full LXX title sequence including the distinctive 'Angel of Great Counsel' and the expanded six-to-seven part divine name list that aligns with the Göttingen LXX apparatus for Isa. 9:6 (LXX 9:5), departing entirely from the MT's different title count and structure; his text is the most complete LXX citation in the patristic tradition for this verse.
citations.theological_use: Cyril uses the complete title list exegetically to map each divine name onto a specific aspect of Christ's person and salvific work, with 'Angel of Great Counsel' anchoring the Son's eternal divine will and 'Mighty God' providing the linchpin of his anti-Nestorian argument that the child born is truly divine.
citations.transmission_implication: Cyril's detailed citation of the full LXX text in the 5th century demonstrates the continued vitality and stability of the LXX textual tradition in Alexandria even as the Vulgate was cementing MT-proximate readings in the West.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation history of Isaiah 9:6 reveals a dominant LXX text form in circulation throughout the Greek-speaking church from the 2nd through 5th centuries, with the LXX-specific 'Angel of Great Counsel' (Μεγάλης Βουλῆς Ἄγγελος) functioning as a near-universal marker of the LXX textual stream, entirely absent from the MT tradition and consistently cited by Irenaeus, Origen, Athanasius, and Cyril. The variation among LXX-using fathers in the number and order of the divine titles — and particularly Eusebius's omission of 'Angel of Great Counsel' compared to Origen's retention of it — attests to a pluriform LXX manuscript tradition for this verse that the Göttingen critical apparatus confirms, suggesting multiple LXX recensions were in simultaneous circulation rather than a single fixed text. Jerome's MT-aligned Vulgate rendering represents a conscious exegetical and translational rupture in the late 4th century, introducing a competing western text form that would shape the title count differently from the LXX tradition. Collectively, these citations confirm that Isaiah 9:6 was a site of active textual diversity: the LXX's theologically charged expansion was not a late scribal invention but was already deeply embedded in the earliest Christian scriptural tradition by the mid-2nd century, predating all surviving LXX manuscripts for this passage.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers from the 2nd century onward almost universally cited a Greek translation (the Septuagint) of Isaiah 9:6 that contained an extra title — 'Angel of Great Counsel' — not found in the Hebrew Bible; this shows that the Greek text used by the church was an expanded, theologically richer version of the original Hebrew. Jerome, writing in the late 4th century, broke with this tradition by going back to the Hebrew, producing the Latin translation that would dominate Western Christianity and give the verse its more familiar five-title form. The difference between these two traditions — Greek with extra titles, Latin closer to Hebrew — is not a medieval development but goes back to the earliest centuries of the church.

notable_variants.reading: Μεγάλης Βουλῆς Ἄγγελος (Angel of Great Counsel) as the first divine title
notable_variants.significance: This title is entirely absent from the MT and constitutes the most striking LXX expansion in this verse; its consistent citation across geographically and chronologically diverse fathers confirms it was embedded in the LXX Vorlage from very early and was not a later scribal addition, a conclusion supported by the Göttingen LXX apparatus which witnesses it in Codex Vaticanus and allied manuscripts.

notable_variants.reading: Six-to-seven part divine name sequence vs. MT's differently structured compound name
notable_variants.significance: The LXX's expansion of the MT's compound name into a sequence of discrete divine titles represents a significant interpretive tradition; patristic use of this expanded sequence as the basis for systematic Christological argument demonstrates that the LXX text form, not the MT, shaped the theological vocabulary of early Christian doctrine regarding Christ's divine attributes.

notable_variants.reading: Absence of 'Angel of Great Counsel' in Eusebius despite LXX affiliation
notable_variants.significance: Eusebius's omission of this distinctive LXX title while otherwise following the LXX suggests access to a hexaplaric or partially Hebrew-corrected recension of the LXX, providing patristic evidence for the kind of recensional activity Origen conducted in the Hexapla and its subsequent influence on 4th-century scriptural manuscripts in Caesarea.

notable_variants.reading: MT-aligned five-title sequence without 'Angel of Great Counsel' (Vulgate: Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis, Pater futuri saeculi, Princeps pacis)
notable_variants.significance: Jerome's deliberate alignment with the Hebrew against the LXX in this verse marks an epochal moment in the textual history of this passage for the western church; by adopting iuxta Hebraeos principles, Jerome created a text that would define the western Catholic tradition of Isaiah 9:6 and later inform the KJV tradition, permanently differentiating it from the Orthodox tradition rooted in the LXX.

bibcrit_assessment.title: LXX 'Angel of Great Counsel' predates all surviving manuscripts
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The single most significant finding from this patristic citation history is that the LXX's distinctive title 'Angel of Great Counsel' was already in widespread, geographically diverse patristic use by the mid-2nd century — generations before any surviving LXX manuscript of Isaiah — confirming that this expansion was not a late scribal or Christian interpolation into the LXX but was part of the LXX textual tradition the church inherited, a conclusion that strengthens the Göttingen LXX apparatus's inclusion of this reading as primary. Furthermore, the variation among fathers in their title sequences documents the pre-recension plurality of the LXX text of this verse in a way no manuscript tradition alone could establish.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Early Christian writers quoting Isaiah 9:6 prove that the Greek Bible's extra title — 'Angel of Great Counsel' — was already part of the text Christians inherited in the 100s CE, long before any surviving Greek Old Testament manuscript; this means the title is genuinely ancient and was not added later by Christian scribes. The patristic evidence also shows that even within the Greek tradition there were small but real differences in how the verse was worded, revealing that the biblical text was not rigidly uniform in the early church.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis correctly identifies the central LXX/MT divergence regarding 'Angel of Great Counsel,' but contains several specific patristic citation references and attributions that range from imprecise to likely fabricated.
